title: Atomics & concurrent collections
scopeHtml: CAS and atomics, LongAdder, ConcurrentHashMap internals and pitfalls, copy-on-write, blocking queues, lock-free structures, Disruptor idea, producer-consumer design.

questions.promptHtml: What is compare-and-swap, and how do the java.util.concurrent.atomic classes use it to be thread-safe without locks?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you know the primitive that every lock-free structure in the JDK is built on, not just the class names.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CAS is a single CPU instruction: "set this memory location to NEW only if it currently equals EXPECTED, and tell me whether it worked". Atomic classes wrap a volatile field and run a loop: read the current value, compute the new one, CAS it in, retry if another thread got there first. No thread ever blocks or sleeps, so there is no lock to hold or deadlock on, but under heavy contention threads burn CPU on retries.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
On x86 CAS is LOCK CMPXCHG; on ARM it is an LL/SC pair (ldxr/stxr) or the CAS instruction in ARMv8.1. HotSpot exposes it via Unsafe/VarHandle intrinsics; AtomicInteger.compareAndSet is a thin wrapper over that.

getAndIncrement():
  loop:
    old = value            // volatile read
    new = old + 1
    if CAS(value, old, new) return old   // success
    // else someone else changed it: retry

Notes: (1) in modern JDKs getAndIncrement compiles straight to LOCK XADD on x86, which cannot fail, so no loop; updateAndGet/accumulateAndGet still use the CAS loop. (2) A CAS also acts as a full memory barrier on x86 and has volatile read+write semantics in the JMM, so it gives visibility and ordering, not only atomicity. (3) The function you pass to updateAndGet may run more than once, so it must be side-effect free.

Lock-free means "some thread always makes progress"; an individual thread can still starve in its retry loop.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger;

AtomicInteger hits = new AtomicInteger();
hits.incrementAndGet();                       // atomic
hits.updateAndGet(v -> Math.min(v + 1, 100)); // CAS loop, lambda must be pure

// Broken: lambda with side effect, may run several times
hits.updateAndGet(v -> { log.info("setting"); return v + 1; });

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Doing if (a.get() == 0) a.set(1): check-then-act on two separate atomic operations. Use compareAndSet(0, 1).
  • Composing two atomics (balance and count) and assuming the pair is atomic. It is not; use one immutable holder in an AtomicReference or a lock.
  • Side effects inside the update lambda.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a CAS loop always faster than a lock? → No. Uncontended yes; under heavy contention failed CAS retries waste CPU and cache-line bouncing dominates. A lock parks losers instead.
  2. What memory semantics does CAS give? → Volatile read and write semantics (JMM); weakCompareAndSet* variants in VarHandle relax that.
  3. What is the ABA problem? → See B1-Q155.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE says "atomic classes are lock-free using CAS". Senior explains the retry loop, that contended CAS burns CPU and bounces cache lines, that lambdas must be pure, and that atomics only protect one variable, not invariants across several.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams replace synchronized counters with AtomicLong and see no gain at 32 threads because the single cache line is the bottleneck (see B1-Q156).

questions.promptHtml: volatile int count; count++ from 10 threads loses updates. Why, and what are the fixes?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Separates visibility from atomicity, the most common concurrency misconception.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: volatile guarantees visibility and ordering, not atomicity. count++ is three steps: read, add, write. Two threads can both read 5 and both write 6, losing an increment. Fix with AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet(), LongAdder for hot counters, or a lock.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
T1: read 5            T2: read 5
T1: write 6           T2: write 6    -> expected 7, got 6

Volatile makes every read see the latest write and prevents reordering around it, but the read-modify-write sequence between them is still interleavable. Volatile is fine for a single-writer flag or a safely published reference (volatile boolean running), or when new value does not depend on the old one. Memory-model detail is owned by the JMM chunk; here the point is the fix choice:

Need Tool
Single counter, moderate contention AtomicInteger/Long
Hot write-mostly counter, read rarely LongAdder
Several variables updated together lock or immutable snapshot in AtomicReference
Flag, single writer volatile

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Broken { volatile int n; void inc() { n++; } }          // lost updates
class Fixed  { final AtomicInteger n = new AtomicInteger(); void inc() { n.incrementAndGet(); } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing volatile on a long/double also makes ++ atomic.
  • "It worked in my test": a 2-thread test on a laptop may hide the race; stress with jcstress or many threads.
  • Making a collection field volatile and assuming its contents are thread-safe. Volatile covers the reference only.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not just synchronized? → Correct, but heavier under contention and can block; atomics suit single variables.
  2. Is volatile long read atomic on 32-bit JVMs? → Yes, volatile makes long/double reads and writes atomic; non-volatile ones may tear per the JLS.
  3. Can volatile fix double-checked locking? → Yes from Java 5 on; owned by the JMM chunk.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "volatile isn't atomic, use Atomic". Senior adds the interleaving, the single-writer exception, and chooses LongAdder vs AtomicLong vs lock by the invariant and contention.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A request-counter metric on a shared volatile long under-reported by ~15% at 8 threads and was blamed on the monitoring agent for a week.

questions.promptHtml: What is the ABA problem in CAS-based algorithms, and how do you solve it in Java?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand that CAS compares values, not history.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CAS only checks "is it still equal to what I read". If another thread changes A to B and back to A, my CAS succeeds although the state changed underneath me, which can corrupt structures like lock-free stacks that reuse nodes. In Java, AtomicStampedReference pairs the reference with an int version stamp, and AtomicMarkableReference pairs it with a boolean. Garbage collection already removes the worst form of ABA, because a node cannot be reused while someone still references it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Classic lock-free stack pop: thread 1 reads head = A, next = B, is preempted. Thread 2 pops A, pops B, pushes A back (now A.next = null, B is gone). Thread 1 resumes: CAS(head, A, B) succeeds, but B is already removed, so head points to a dead node.

In languages with manual memory management, A's address can be recycled. In Java, A cannot be reclaimed while thread 1 holds it, but if code reuses node objects from a pool or if values (not identities) are compared, ABA is real. Also logical ABA: a counter that goes 5 -> 6 -> 5, where intermediate state matters.

Fix: version the value.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicStampedReference;

AtomicStampedReference<Node> head = new AtomicStampedReference<>(null, 0);
int[] stampHolder = new int[1];
Node cur = head.get(stampHolder);
int stamp = stampHolder[0];
boolean ok = head.compareAndSet(cur, cur.next, stamp, stamp + 1);

Note: compareAndSet on AtomicStampedReference compares references with ==, not equals.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using AtomicReference<Integer> / boxed values and comparing identity of cached boxes (Integer cache -128..127) giving surprising successes or failures.
  • Assuming GC makes ABA impossible. It prevents address reuse, not value or pooled-object reuse.
  • Forgetting AtomicStampedReference allocates a pair object per update.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does ConcurrentLinkedQueue suffer ABA? → Not in practice; it allocates fresh nodes and GC prevents reuse.
  2. When would you use AtomicMarkableReference? → When you need a logical-delete flag with the pointer, as in lock-free linked list deletion (Harris).
  3. How do native/off-heap lock-free structures handle it? → Tagged pointers, hazard pointers, or epoch reclamation.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE defines A-B-A. Senior shows the stack-pop corruption, explains why Java's GC narrows but doesn't eliminate it, and mentions stamps vs pooling avoidance.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Rare in app code; it shows up in hand-rolled object pools and custom lock-free queues, where it appears as occasional lost or duplicated items.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use LongAdder instead of AtomicLong, and what is the cost?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of contention, cache lines, and trade-offs, not API trivia.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: AtomicLong is one variable that every thread CASes, so under heavy write contention threads fight over one cache line and retry. LongAdder keeps a base plus a lazily grown array of cells; each thread tends to hit its own cell, so adds scale with cores. Reading with sum() adds all cells, is not an atomic snapshot, and the class uses more memory. Use it for write-heavy, read-rarely statistics counters, not for sequence generators or anything needing compare-and-set.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
LongAdder extends Striped64. add(x): try CAS on base; if that fails (contention), pick a cell by a per-thread probe hash and CAS there; if that fails too, rehash or grow the cells array (power of two, bounded by the number of CPUs). Cells are @Contended padded to avoid false sharing between them. The Javadoc states: under low contention both are similar; under high contention throughput is significantly higher at the expense of more space.

AtomicLong:  T1 T2 T3 T4 -> [ value ]            (1 cache line, bounced between cores)
LongAdder:   T1->[c0] T2->[c1] T3->[c2] T4->[base]   sum() = base + c0 + c1 + c2

Trade-offs: sum() can miss concurrent updates (weakly consistent); no get-then-CAS, so no unique IDs or bounded counters; reset()/sumThenReset() are only safe when no concurrent updates. Related: LongAccumulator for max/min with a commutative function, DoubleAdder. Micrometer and many metrics libs use LongAdder internally.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder;

LongAdder requests = new LongAdder();
requests.increment();            // hot path, many threads
long total = requests.sum();     // metrics scrape, approximate under writes

// Wrong for IDs: no atomic "read and bump"
// long id = adder.sumThenReset(); // not safe for sequence generation

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using LongAdder for a sequence number or a rate limiter permit counter that needs exact check-then-update.
  • Calling sum() in the hot path (it walks the cells).
  • Switching without measuring: with 2-4 threads the gain is negligible and memory use grows.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why are cells padded? → Adjacent cells would share a cache line (false sharing) and recreate the contention.
  2. Is sum() exact? → Only when no concurrent updates; otherwise a moving approximation.
  3. How would you build a bounded counter with striping? → Hard; you need a global invariant, so use a Semaphore or accept approximate limits with local budgets.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "LongAdder is faster". Senior explains cell striping, @Contended, non-atomic sum(), memory cost, and the use cases it can't serve.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A request-metrics counter on a 64-core host showed up as the top frame in async-profiler (CAS retry loop); swapping to LongAdder dropped its CPU share from ~9% to under 1% (see B1-Q173).

questions.promptHtml: How do you update a multi-field piece of shared state atomically without a lock? Explain the AtomicReference pattern and its limits.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the "immutable snapshot + CAS" idiom and awareness of its cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Put all the related fields in one immutable object and keep it in an AtomicReference. To update, read the reference, build a new object from it, and compareAndSet(old, new) in a loop. Readers always see a consistent snapshot. The limits: the update function must be pure and cheap because it may run multiple times, writers can livelock-ish under contention, and each update allocates.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Two atomics don't make a pair atomic. One immutable record does, since the single reference swap is the linearization point. AtomicReference.updateAndGet and accumulateAndGet wrap the loop. CAS on references uses identity (==), so the expected value must be the exact object you read.

Where it fits: config hot-reload, routing tables, rate-limiter state (tokens + timestamp), circuit-breaker state. Where it breaks: large state (copying 1 MB per update), highly contended writes (retry storms), or updates with side effects (you cannot undo a half-done external call).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicReference;

record Bucket(long tokens, long lastRefillNanos) {}

class TokenBucket {
    private final AtomicReference<Bucket> state = new AtomicReference<>(new Bucket(10, System.nanoTime()));

    boolean tryAcquire() {
        while (true) {
            Bucket cur = state.get();
            Bucket next = refill(cur);               // pure function, no I/O
            if (next.tokens() <= 0) return false;
            Bucket updated = new Bucket(next.tokens() - 1, next.lastRefillNanos());
            if (state.compareAndSet(cur, updated)) return true;
        }
    }
    private Bucket refill(Bucket b) { /* compute from time, no side effects */ return b; }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Mutable fields in the held object (a List inside the record being mutated) which defeats the pattern.
  • Doing I/O or logging inside the update function.
  • Expecting equals semantics from compareAndSet.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not synchronized? → Also fine; the CAS version gives lock-free reads and no blocking, but costs allocation.
  2. How do you avoid retry storms? → Reduce contention (shard), or use a lock when writers are many and updates are heavy.
  3. Does this solve ABA? → Fresh objects each time avoid pooled reuse; use stamps if you recycle.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE knows AtomicReference. Senior designs the immutable snapshot, states the purity requirement, and names when a plain lock beats it.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Hot-reloaded routing config via AtomicReference<Config> removed a read lock from a 50k RPS path.

questions.contextHtml:
A service caches per-tenant rate limiters. Under load (8 Tomcat threads per pod, 1,200 RPS), you notice that two requests for a new tenant sometimes end up with different limiter instances and the tenant exceeds quota by up to 2x right after first access. The code:

private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, RateLimiter> limiters = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

RateLimiter limiterFor(String tenant) {
    if (!limiters.containsKey(tenant)) {
        limiters.put(tenant, RateLimiter.create(100)); // 100 permits/s
    }
    return limiters.get(tenant);
}

The map is thread-safe, tests pass, and a code reviewer said "it's a ConcurrentHashMap, it's fine". Another dev suggests wrapping the method in synchronized.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you fix it, and what would you NOT do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe so the bug must be in RateLimiter", or "make the method synchronized". The first misses compound operations; the second works but serializes all tenants on a global lock.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is creating a RateLimiter expensive or side-effecting (registers metrics, starts a thread)? Can limiters be evicted? Are all calls via this method? These decide whether double-create is merely wasteful or harmful.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Replace the check-then-put with computeIfAbsent, a one-line hotfix.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) check-then-act race: two threads both see absent, both put, last write wins, and the first caller keeps using the discarded instance; (b) a different limiter keyed with inconsistent tenant string (case, whitespace); (c) clock skew in the limiter. (a) matches "only right after first access".
  4. How I'd verify each: A unit test with a CountDownLatch releasing 32 threads on the same new key and counting distinct instances (identityHashCode); log limiter creation per tenant; for (b) log the raw key.
  5. Root cause: ConcurrentHashMap makes each single call atomic, not the sequence containsKey + put. Interleaving: T1 absent, T2 absent, T1 put(L1), T2 put(L2), T1 returns L1 (via get it may see L2, but a thread that held L1 earlier from putIfAbsent-less patterns diverges). Instances differ, so quotas multiply.
  6. Fix:
RateLimiter limiterFor(String tenant) {
    return limiters.computeIfAbsent(tenant, t -> RateLimiter.create(100));
}

computeIfAbsent is atomic per key and the function runs once. Keep the function short and free of map access. If creation were expensive or blocking, use putIfAbsent with a lazily built holder (e.g. Lazy wrapper) so the heavy work is outside the bin lock. 7. Prevention: Static-analysis rule (Error Prone has checks for check-then-act on concurrent maps; verify exact name), code review checklist item "compound action on concurrent collection", a concurrency test with a latch. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not synchronized on the method (serializes unrelated tenants); not synchronized(limiters) either. Not putIfAbsent(tenant, RateLimiter.create(100)) blindly if construction is costly, since it allocates on every call even when present.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if RateLimiter.create takes 200 ms (loads config over network)? → Do not run it inside computeIfAbsent; it blocks other updates in that bin. Use a CompletableFuture/lazy holder value and putIfAbsent.
  • What if two limiters were created and one was discarded and it registered a metric? → Leaks; registration must be idempotent or done after winning.
  • Why does get after put not save you? → Another thread's put may replace yours between your put and get, and another thread may already hold your discarded instance.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A per-customer client cache created two HTTP clients for each new customer under burst; the discarded one was never closed and leaked 300 sockets per deploy until someone grepped for containsKey + put.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: believes the map is enough, or fixes with a global synchronized.
  • Hire: identifies check-then-act, uses computeIfAbsent/putIfAbsent.
  • Strong hire: also discusses side-effecting/expensive value creation, per-bin blocking, and a latch-based regression test.

questions.promptHtml: How does ConcurrentHashMap work internally in Java 8+, and how is it different from the Java 7 design?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A standard senior question: tests whether you know the real concurrency mechanism (CAS plus per-bin locks) rather than "it has segments".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Java 7 split the table into 16 Segments, each a lock. Java 8 removed segments: there is one array of bins. Inserting into an empty bin is a lock-free CAS of the first node; if the bin is occupied, I synchronized on that bin's head node, so writers only contend when they hit the same bin. Reads (get) take no locks and rely on volatile fields. Long bins turn into red-black trees, and resize is cooperative: threads that hit a moved bin help transfer it.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Hash: spread(h) = (h ^ (h >>> 16)) & 0x7fffffff, index = (n-1) & hash, same idea as HashMap. Table size is a power of two (default 16, lazily created); resize threshold is 0.75 * n (sizeCtl).
  • putVal: if table null -> init (CAS on sizeCtl). If bin empty -> casTabAt the new node, no lock. If the head hash is MOVED (a ForwardingNode) -> helpTransfer. Else synchronized (f) on the first node, walk the list or tree, replace or append. After insert, if bin count >= TREEIFY_THRESHOLD (8) call treeifyBin, which resizes instead if the table is smaller than MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY (64). I state these constants from the source as I know it; verify against your JDK.
  • get: no lock; node val and next are volatile, table slots read with volatile semantics. Sees either the old or new state of a bin, never a torn one.
  • Counting: baseCount plus a CounterCell[] (striped like LongAdder). size() sums them.
  • Resize: a new table of 2n; threads claim stride ranges of old bins; each transferred bin gets a ForwardingNode so readers redirect to the new table and writers help.
  • No null keys or values: get returning null must unambiguously mean "absent" without a lock.
table: [0][1][2][3]...[n-1]
        |  |     |
       null A->B  TreeBin(red-black)
 empty: CAS      occupied: synchronized(head)

Java 7 vs 8: segments (default concurrency level 16, fixed at construction) vs per-bin locking (concurrency scales with table size), tree bins, cooperative resize, striped counter.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ConcurrentHashMap<String,Integer> m = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
m.merge("k", 1, Integer::sum);   // atomic per key

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "it locks the whole map" (that's Hashtable / synchronizedMap) or "16 segments" (Java 7).
  • Assuming iteration or size() is a consistent snapshot.
  • Expecting null values to work (NPE).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is get lock-free and still correct? → Volatile reads of node fields and table slots plus safe publication through CAS/lock; readers see a fully built node.
  2. Why does it ban null? → To make get() == null unambiguous without a containsKey that would not be atomic with get.
  3. Does concurrencyLevel still matter? → Only as a sizing hint in the constructor in Java 8+.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "segment locks". Senior describes CAS on empty bins, synchronized on the head node, ForwardingNode and helped resize, tree bins and the 64-capacity guard, and striped size counters.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A hot key in one bin serializes writers (all merges on a single key take that bin's lock), which is why one very hot counter should be a LongAdder value (see B1-Q177).

questions.promptHtml: Compare Hashtable, Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) and ConcurrentHashMap. Which do you use and why?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Baseline check that you know why legacy synchronized wrappers are rarely the answer.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Hashtable and synchronizedMap guard every method with one lock (the object's monitor or a mutex), so all threads serialize, and iterating still requires manual locking. ConcurrentHashMap allows concurrent reads without locks and concurrent writes to different bins, offers atomic compound operations (computeIfAbsent, merge), and has weakly consistent iterators that never throw ConcurrentModificationException. I default to ConcurrentHashMap for shared maps.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Hashtable synchronizedMap(HashMap) ConcurrentHashMap
Locking monitor on this per method one mutex per method CAS + per-bin lock, lock-free reads
Null key/value no yes (HashMap rules) no
Iterator fail-fast fail-fast, must hold lock while iterating weakly consistent, no CME
Atomic compound ops none none (you lock externally) putIfAbsent, compute*, merge
size() exact, locked exact, locked approximate under concurrent updates

A synchronized wrapper still leaves check-then-act and iteration unsafe: if (!m.containsKey(k)) m.put(k, v) is two calls. You must synchronized (m) { ... } the whole thing, using the wrapper's own lock (documented for iteration).

Choose a synchronized wrapper only if you need null keys/values, a consistent snapshot size, or are already holding a lock for a compound invariant.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
Map<String,Integer> sm = Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>());
synchronized (sm) {                       // required to iterate safely
    for (var e : sm.entrySet()) { /* ... */ }
}
ConcurrentHashMap<String,Integer> chm = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
chm.forEach((k, v) -> { /* no external lock, no CME */ });

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Iterating a synchronizedMap without locking: ConcurrentModificationException or worse, inconsistent data.
  • Thinking ConcurrentHashMap.size() is exact or that containsKey + put is atomic.
  • Using Hashtable in new code.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does CHM iteration reflect concurrent changes? → Possibly; weakly consistent, reflects state at or after creation, never throws CME.
  2. Is ConcurrentHashMap always faster? → Not for single-threaded or tiny maps; there are extra volatile reads and memory per node.
  3. What about Collections.synchronizedMap iteration over keySet()? → Still requires holding the map's mutex.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "CHM is faster, others lock everything". Senior gives the table, compound-operation gap, null semantics, and iteration/consistency differences.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A synchronizedMap cache iterated by a metrics thread caused rare ConcurrentModificationException in a scheduled job at 02:00 when writers were busy.

questions.promptHtml: What does ConcurrentHashMap.size() actually return under concurrent updates, and what are mappingCount() and weakly consistent iterators? How should you use them in production?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Probes understanding of the consistency model behind concurrent collections, and whether you'd base logic on size().

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: size() is an estimate under concurrent modification: it sums a base counter and striped counter cells without freezing writers, so by the time it returns it may be stale. The Javadoc says such methods are suitable for monitoring, not program control. mappingCount() is the same estimate as a long, preferred for huge maps. Iterators are weakly consistent: they traverse elements as they existed at creation and may or may not reflect later changes, but never throw CME or return an element twice.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Counting uses baseCount plus CounterCell[] (same idea as LongAdder), sumCount() adds them. Adds on the put path either CAS baseCount or a cell. There is no global lock, so size() isn't linearizable with respect to concurrent updates; with no concurrent updates it is exact. isEmpty() is sumCount() <= 0.

So "if (map.size() < MAX) map.put(k, v)" is a bound check that can overshoot: N threads see size = MAX-1 and all insert. For a hard capacity use a Semaphore/AtomicInteger reservation, a lock, or LinkedHashMap under a lock (or Caffeine, which handles eviction asynchronously).

Bulk ops (forEach, reduce, search) take parallelismThreshold: Long.MAX_VALUE forces sequential; 1 maximum parallelism using ForkJoinPool.commonPool(). Don't pass 1 casually in a web server; the common pool is shared (see the pool chunk).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// BROKEN: bound can be exceeded under concurrency
if (cache.size() < 10_000) cache.put(key, val);

// Better: reserve a slot first
private final AtomicInteger slots = new AtomicInteger();
boolean tryPut(K k, V v) {
    if (slots.incrementAndGet() > 10_000) { slots.decrementAndGet(); return false; }
    if (cache.putIfAbsent(k, v) != null) slots.decrementAndGet();
    return true;
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using size() for admission control or loop termination.
  • Expecting iteration to be a snapshot ("copy" it with new ArrayList<>(map.values()) if you need approximate point-in-time, and know even that copy is iterated weakly).
  • Passing parallelism threshold 1 on a request thread.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not make size() exact? → It would need a global lock or stop-the-world, destroying the scalability.
  2. Does Collections.synchronizedMap give exact size()? → Yes, since every op takes the same lock.
  3. Can a weakly consistent iterator skip an existing element? → It can miss entries added after creation; an element present throughout the traversal is returned once.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "size is approximate". Senior explains the counter design, why bound checks overshoot, safe alternatives, and the bulk-op threshold/common-pool risk.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "max 5,000 sessions" check using size() admitted ~5,300 during a login burst; the downstream limit was hit anyway.

questions.contextHtml:
A pricing service (Java 17, 16 vCPU, 4 GB heap, 2,500 RPS) memoizes expensive rule evaluations:

ConcurrentHashMap<String, Rule> rules = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

Rule resolve(String id) {
    return rules.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> {
        Rule r = loadFromDb(k);                 // 120 ms, p99 900 ms
        for (String dep : r.dependencies())
            r.link(resolve(dep));               // recursive, same map
        return r;
    });
}

After a deploy that added rules with dependencies, p99 jumped from 80 ms to 12 s for some tenants, CPU on two pods sat at 100% and a few request threads never returned. jstack shows several threads in ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent and others BLOCKED/RUNNABLE in ConcurrentHashMap.transfer and ConcurrentHashMap.putVal. Heap and GC are normal. Someone says "the DB is slow".
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose and fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the DB, adds more threads or a bigger DB pool. Misses that the function runs while holding a bin lock and that it modifies the same map.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which Java version (behaviour of recursive update changed between 8 and 9+)? Do dependencies ever form cycles? What is the DB pool size and wait time? When did it begin relative to the deploy?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Roll back the deploy (or feature-flag off rules with dependencies), restart the wedged pods after capturing 3 thread dumps 5 s apart.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) recursive computeIfAbsent on the same map, hitting a bin the thread already holds or a resize in progress (documented as prohibited); (b) a slow DB call executed inside the bin lock, blocking other keys that hash to the same bin; (c) a dependency cycle (A -> B -> A) that never terminates; (d) DB pool exhaustion. 100% CPU with threads spinning in transfer/putVal fits (a)/(c) rather than DB slowness.
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd <pid> Thread.print x3 and compare stack frames; async-profiler -e cpu to see where the spin is; log recursion depth; Hikari pool metrics (active/pending) to rule out (d); check whether dependency graph has cycles with an offline script.
  5. Root cause: The Javadoc requires the mapping function to be short and not to update the map. A recursive computeIfAbsent can either throw IllegalStateException("Recursive update") in cases the JDK detects, or deadlock/spin when it doesn't (the exact behaviour is JDK-version dependent; Java 8 could loop forever, later versions detect more cases; verify per JDK). In addition, the DB call runs while the bin head is locked, so unrelated keys in the same bin stall.
  6. Fix: Short term: compute outside the map and publish:
Rule resolve(String id) {
    Rule cached = rules.get(id);
    if (cached != null) return cached;
    Rule r = build(id, new HashSet<>());     // load + resolve deps, cycle check, no map locks
    Rule prev = rules.putIfAbsent(id, r);
    return prev != null ? prev : r;
}

Long term: cache values as CompletableFuture<Rule> / a Caffeine AsyncLoadingCache so loading is deduplicated without holding bin locks, with cycle detection and a bounded timeout. 7. Prevention: Code-review rule "no map access and no I/O inside compute functions"; a unit test with deep dependency chains and a cycle; alert on p99 and on request thread count in RUNNABLE inside CHM frames. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a global lock (hides the bug, serializes). Not raising pool size. The putIfAbsent approach may load the same rule twice under a race; acceptable if loading is idempotent, otherwise use the future-valued cache.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if loading must happen exactly once? → Future-valued map: computeIfAbsent(id, k -> new CompletableFuture<>()) then complete it outside the lock by the winner.
  • Why did only some tenants break? → Only those whose rules have dependencies and whose ids share a bin or recurse.
  • What if you cannot upgrade Java? → Same fix; the pattern is wrong on every version.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "config tree resolver" memoized with a recursive computeIfAbsent worked in staging because its tests used flat configs; production's nested configs froze two nodes at 100% CPU for 40 minutes.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames DB or scales out.
  • Hire: spots recursive compute and I/O in the lambda, fixes with get/putIfAbsent.
  • Strong hire: explains per-bin locking, JDK-version behaviour, future-valued or Caffeine design, cycle detection, thread-dump verification.

questions.promptHtml: How does CopyOnWriteArrayList work and when is it the right (or wrong) choice?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests trade-off thinking: read/write ratio, iteration semantics, memory and GC cost.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It stores elements in an array that's never modified in place. Every write takes a lock, copies the whole array, applies the change, and swaps the volatile reference. Readers just read the current array reference, lock-free. Iterators work on the array snapshot at creation, so they never throw CME and never see later writes. It's ideal for small, read-mostly collections like listener lists; terrible for write-heavy or large ones, since each write is O(n) and allocates.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
array ref --> [a][b][c]
add(d): lock; new [a][b][c][d]; array = new; unlock   (old array stays valid for existing iterators)

Consequences: iterator remove/set/add throw UnsupportedOperationException; iteration sees stale data by design; writes are serialized (single lock) and allocate n+1 slots, which raises young-gen pressure; large arrays may land in humongous territory in G1 (see GC chunks) at roughly more than half a region. addIfAbsent and CopyOnWriteArraySet exist for set semantics (O(n) lookup).

Cost example: 10,000 elements of 8 bytes (compressed refs 4 bytes) is about 40 KB per write copy. At 1,000 writes/s that's about 40 MB/s of garbage just from the list.

Use: event listener registries, route lists reloaded rarely. Avoid: queues, caches with frequent puts, sessions.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
CopyOnWriteArrayList<Listener> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
void fire(Event e) {
    for (Listener l : listeners) l.on(e);   // snapshot, safe even if a listener unregisters itself
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it as a general thread-safe list for a write-heavy workload.
  • Calling iterator.remove().
  • Expecting iteration to reflect an add made by another thread mid-loop.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Alternatives for write-heavy lists? → ConcurrentLinkedQueue, Collections.synchronizedList, or redesign with an immutable snapshot in AtomicReference rebuilt in batches.
  2. Is it consistent with happens-before? → Writes publish via volatile array reference; actions before an add happen-before accesses after the element is seen.
  3. How does it compare to ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet()? → CHM-set has O(1) ops and no copy but unordered and weakly consistent.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "good for reads, copies on write". Senior quantifies copy cost, notes garbage/GC impact, iterator semantics, and picks alternatives.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A listener list that grew to 40k entries (leaked registrations) turned each register call into a 160 KB copy and spiked allocation rate.

questions.promptHtml: Why does ConcurrentModificationException happen, even in single-threaded code? How do fail-fast and weakly consistent iterators differ?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Very common basic question with a trap: CME is not about threads.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ArrayList/HashMap keep a modCount that every structural change increments; the iterator remembers the value at creation and checks it on next(). If the collection changed by anything other than the iterator itself, it throws CME. That can happen on one thread (removing inside a for-each). It's best-effort detection, not a thread-safety guarantee. Concurrent collections use weakly consistent iterators: no CME, they reflect some state at or after creation.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Fail-fast: ArrayList, HashMap, HashSet, LinkedList. Check modCount != expectedModCount in next() (for ArrayList, hasNext() is cursor != size, so removing the second-to-last element in a for-each silently skips the check and exits cleanly, a known quirk).
  • Weakly consistent: ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentLinkedQueue, ConcurrentSkipListMap. No CME, no duplicates, may or may not see concurrent changes.
  • Snapshot: CopyOnWriteArrayList, iterates over the array captured at creation.

Fixes for single-thread removal: iterator.remove(), removeIf, collect-then-remove, or a stream into a new list.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
List<Integer> xs = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4));
for (Integer x : xs) if (x == 2) xs.remove(x);   // CME on next()
xs.removeIf(x -> x == 2);                         // correct

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Wrapping in try/catch for CME instead of fixing the logic.
  • Believing CME proves a race (no) or its absence proves safety (no, detection is best-effort).
  • synchronizedList iteration without holding the lock.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does HashMap.forEach check modCount? → Yes, throws CME at end if modified.
  2. Is it safe to remove from a ConcurrentHashMap while iterating? → Yes.
  3. Is the missing CME a guarantee of correctness? → No; the Javadoc says fail-fast is best effort and must not be relied on for correctness.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "modify while iterating". Senior explains modCount, the ArrayList second-to-last quirk, best-effort nature, and picks the right iterator model.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A scheduled cleanup removing expired entries from a shared HashMap threw CME only under load; the real bug was unsynchronized sharing (data race), not the iteration.

questions.promptHtml: Walk through the BlockingQueue implementations (ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue, PriorityBlockingQueue, LinkedTransferQueue, LinkedBlockingDeque) and how you'd choose among them.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks that you know bounded vs unbounded, locking design, and the backpressure implications.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ArrayBlockingQueue is a bounded ring buffer with one lock for both ends. LinkedBlockingQueue is linked nodes with separate put and take locks, optionally bounded (default capacity is Integer.MAX_VALUE, effectively unbounded). PriorityBlockingQueue is unbounded and orders by priority. LinkedBlockingDeque is a double-ended, bounded-optional queue. LinkedTransferQueue is unbounded and lock-free with transfer() handoff. I choose bounded for backpressure, and unbounded only if the producer is naturally limited.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Queue Bound Locking Notes
ArrayBlockingQueue required one ReentrantLock, 2 conditions preallocated array, optional fairness, predictable memory
LinkedBlockingQueue optional putLock + takeLock, atomic count higher throughput with split locks; allocates a node per element
PriorityBlockingQueue unbounded one lock heap; not FIFO among equals; can OOM
LinkedBlockingDeque optional one lock work stealing / both ends
SynchronousQueue none (capacity 0) handoff see B1-Q167
DelayQueue unbounded one lock see B1-Q167
LinkedTransferQueue unbounded lock-free CAS transfer, tryTransfer

API families: put/take block; offer/poll return immediately (or with timeout); add/remove throw.

Rule: an unbounded queue turns overload into memory growth and latency, not rejection. A bounded queue surfaces overload at the producer, which is where you can shed or slow down.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
BlockingQueue<Job> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000);
if (!q.offer(job, 50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) {
    throw new RejectedExecutionException("queue full");   // explicit backpressure
}
Job j = q.take();

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• new LinkedBlockingQueue<>() thinking it is bounded.
  • size() used for decisions; it is racy.
  • Using PriorityBlockingQueue and expecting stable ordering for equal priorities.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why two locks in LinkedBlockingQueue? → Producers and consumers rarely conflict, so throughput improves; they coordinate via an AtomicInteger count.
  2. When is fairness worth it? → To avoid starving waiting threads at a throughput cost; rarely.
  3. Which feeds ThreadPoolExecutor best? → A bounded one with a rejection policy that applies backpressure (see B1-Q166).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE lists the classes. Senior ties them to backpressure, memory predictability, lock structure, and operational failure modes.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue between an Kafka consumer and a slow writer grew to 6 GB before the pod was OOM-killed.

questions.contextHtml: A notification service (Java 17, 2 GB container, -Xmx1g, 3 pods) uses Executors.newFixedThreadPool(16) to send emails/webhooks. A partner SMTP gateway degrades: each send goes from 40 ms to 8 s. Inbound rate stays 600 tasks/s. Over 25 minutes: heap climbs from 300 MB to 1 GB, GC logs show repeated full GCs (Pause Full (G1 Compaction Pause) 950ms), then java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space, pods restart, and the queued notifications are lost. CPU was low throughout; the API itself returned 200 to callers the whole time. The team's first idea: "double the pool to 32 threads".
questions.promptHtml: Explain what happened and redesign.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Increase heap/threads. Doesn't realize newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded queue, so overload turns into memory growth instead of an error.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must notifications survive restart (durability)? Can the API return 429/503 under overload? Is it idempotent to retry? What does a task retain (payload size)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cut traffic to the degraded gateway (circuit breaker/feature flag), scale out or temporarily raise memory, drain via a dead-letter store if needed.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue backing the fixed pool absorbing the backlog: 16 threads / 8 s = 2 tasks/s per pod-pool... precisely 16/8 = 2 completions/s vs 600 in, so the backlog grows ~598 tasks/s; (b) memory leak elsewhere; (c) GC misconfiguration. Math: 598/s x 1500 s = ~900k queued tasks; at ~1 KB each = ~0.9 GB, matching the heap.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump / jmap -histo shows millions of FutureTask/Runnable instances held by LinkedBlockingQueue$Node; expose ThreadPoolExecutor.getQueue().size() and getActiveCount() via Micrometer; MAT dominator tree.
  5. Root cause: Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) = ThreadPoolExecutor(n, n, 0, ms, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()), an effectively unbounded queue (capacity Integer.MAX_VALUE), so maximumPoolSize and rejection never trigger. Arrival rate (600/s) exceeded service rate (2/s) by 300x, and no backpressure signal existed.
  6. Fix: Short term: bounded ArrayBlockingQueue and an explicit policy.
ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    16, 16, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS,
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2_000),
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.AbortPolicy());     // or custom: persist to outbox, return 503

Add per-call timeouts (3 s) and a circuit breaker on the gateway. Long term: durable outbox/Kafka topic with a consumer pulling at its own pace so backpressure lives in the broker. 7. Prevention: Alert on queue depth and rejection count; ban Executors.new* factories via lint (Alibaba P3C and Error Prone-style rules exist; verify tooling), load test with a slowed dependency. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not "just more threads" (the slow dependency gets 2x more requests and may fail harder). CallerRunsPolicy slows producers but runs SMTP calls on request threads; fine only if that is intended. Dropping tasks silently is worse than failing loudly.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What queue size? → Size from tolerated latency: queue = rate x acceptable wait; e.g. 600/s x 3 s tolerance but per-pod 200/s x 3 s = 600; 2,000 gives headroom. Justify with Little's law (see pool-sizing chunk).
  • Why not SynchronousQueue? → It would force unbounded thread creation unless max is bounded; also rejection when all max threads busy, a legitimate alternative.
  • Cached thread pool for this? → Same hazard in a different dimension: unbounded threads (OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An "async audit logger" with a fixed pool hid a slow storage backend for hours; the first symptom was GC time, not errors, because the queue silently held 20 million events.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases threads/heap.
  • Hire: identifies unbounded queue, switches to bounded with rejection.
  • Strong hire: does the arrival/service-rate math, adds circuit breaker, outbox/broker design, and queue-depth alerting.

questions.promptHtml: What are SynchronousQueue and DelayQueue, how do they work, and where are they used inside the JDK or in real designs?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests whether you understand the less common queues that underpin newCachedThreadPool and scheduling/expiry designs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: SynchronousQueue has zero capacity: a put blocks until a take arrives and vice versa, a direct handoff. Executors.newCachedThreadPool uses it, so a task either goes to an idle thread or triggers a new thread. DelayQueue is an unbounded priority queue of Delayed elements; take() blocks until the head's delay has expired, so items come out in expiry order. It is a natural fit for expiring entries, retries with backoff, and simple timers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SynchronousQueue: offer(x) returns false unless a consumer is already waiting; poll() returns null unless a producer is waiting. In ThreadPoolExecutor, the Javadoc describes direct handoff as a good default choice that hands tasks to threads without holding them, but it generally requires an unbounded maximumPoolSize to avoid rejection, which means unbounded thread growth under overload. Implementation detail: historically it used dual stacks/queues (lock-free); JDK 21 reimplemented it (verify specifics for your version).

DelayQueue<E extends Delayed>: internally a PriorityQueue guarded by a ReentrantLock; Delayed.getDelay(unit) returns remaining time and compareTo orders by expiry. take() waits on a condition for min(head delay); a leader-follower pattern ensures only one thread waits for the head's delay, others wait indefinitely until signalled, avoiding thundering herds. Unbounded: producers never block.

Caveats: the head's delay uses your clock; use System.nanoTime()-based values, not wall-clock, so clock jumps don't misfire. size() includes unexpired elements. ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor has its own internal DelayedWorkQueue rather than DelayQueue.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
class Retry implements Delayed {
    final Runnable task; final long fireAtNanos;
    Retry(Runnable t, long delayMs) { task = t; fireAtNanos = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS.toNanos(delayMs); }
    public long getDelay(TimeUnit u) { return u.convert(fireAtNanos - System.nanoTime(), TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS); }
    public int compareTo(Delayed o) { return Long.compare(fireAtNanos, ((Retry) o).fireAtNanos); }
}
DelayQueue<Retry> q = new DelayQueue<>();
q.put(new Retry(() -> call(), 500));
q.take().task.run();      // blocks ~500 ms

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Inconsistent compareTo and getDelay, causing wrong ordering or early release.
  • Using wall-clock time.
  • Using SynchronousQueue in a pool with a bounded max pool size and then seeing RejectedExecutionException under bursts.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does the cached pool use SynchronousQueue? → To hand each task to an idle worker or spawn one immediately, with no queueing latency.
  2. How would you build per-key expiry cache with DelayQueue? → Insert (key, expiry) entries; a daemon thread take()s and removes the key if its version still matches; Caffeine does this better with timer wheels.
  3. What is the hazard of a thousand-thread cached pool? → Memory per stack (~1 MB reserved by default on 64-bit Linux, verify) and context-switch cost.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "synchronous hands off, delay waits". Senior ties it to cached-pool behaviour, rejection math, leader-follower waiting, and the nanoTime rule.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Retry scheduling via a DelayQueue lost items on restart; teams later moved to a durable delayed topic.

questions.promptHtml: How does ConcurrentLinkedQueue work, and when would you choose it over a LinkedBlockingQueue?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks understanding of lock-free vs blocking trade-offs and the O(n) size() gotcha.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ConcurrentLinkedQueue is an unbounded, non-blocking FIFO queue based on the Michael-Scott algorithm: head and tail pointers advanced with CAS, no locks. offer and poll never block, so consumers must handle "empty" themselves (spin, sleep, or park). size() is O(n) because it traverses. I choose it for many producers/consumers needing minimal latency with no need for blocking or capacity; when consumers should wait or I need backpressure, I use a BlockingQueue.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Structure: singly-linked nodes; head points to the first live node (or a dummy), tail is a hint that may lag by a step. offer: CAS tail.next from null to new node, then CAS tail forward; if another thread already added, help advance. poll: CAS the head item to null, then unlink. Threads help each other, which gives lock-freedom: at least one thread always completes in finite steps.

Properties:

  • Unbounded, so overload becomes memory growth.
  • Iterators are weakly consistent.
  • size() and isEmpty(): isEmpty() is O(1), size() traverses; both can be stale.
  • Nodes are garbage: allocation per element; no ABA issue because of GC.
  • No take(): use LinkedTransferQueue or a BlockingQueue for waiting.

Blocking vs non-blocking: blocking queues park threads (cheap CPU while idle, higher wake latency, natural flow control). Non-blocking queues give lower latency with active polling, which burns CPU if idle-spinning.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ConcurrentLinkedQueue<Event> q = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();
q.offer(e);
Event next;
while ((next = q.poll()) != null) handle(next);     // drain loop; exits when momentarily empty
// BAD in a hot loop: q.size() is O(n)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Spin-polling forever on an empty queue, pinning a core.
  • Calling size() for metrics every request.
  • Assuming it limits memory.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is it wait-free? → No, lock-free: individual operations may retry.
  2. Why does GC remove ABA concerns here? → Nodes are fresh and not reclaimed while referenced.
  3. Alternative for strict low latency? → Disruptor/ring buffers (B1-Q169) or JCTools queues (verify library fit).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "lock-free queue". Senior notes helping CAS on tail, O(n) size, unboundedness, polling cost, and picks by backpressure needs.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A metrics-sampler pushed events to a CLQ and size() as a gauge turned a 5 ms operation into 400 ms at 2M queued items.

questions.promptHtml: What is the LMAX Disruptor idea, and why can it outperform ArrayBlockingQueue for some workloads? When would you not use it?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests mechanical-sympathy knowledge: false sharing, allocation, cache locality, and contention design.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The Disruptor is a pre-allocated ring buffer with sequence numbers instead of locks. Producers claim a slot by incrementing a sequence, write into a reused event object, then publish; consumers track their own sequence and wait using a configurable strategy (busy-spin, yield, block). Wins come from no locks, no per-event allocation, power-of-two index masking, cache-friendly sequential memory, and padding sequence counters to avoid false sharing. I'd use it for single-digit-microsecond pipelines (trading, high-rate event processing); for ordinary services a blocking queue is simpler and fast enough.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
ring (size 2^k):  [e0][e1][e2]...[e7]   index = seq & (size-1)
producer cursor ---> 12 (published)        consumer A seq: 10    consumer B seq: 9
slowest consumer gates the producer: producer can't wrap past min(consumer seq)

Key design points (from the project's published design as summarized in several write-ups; verify against the official docs/technical paper before quoting numbers):

  1. Single-writer principle: one producer thread per sequence avoids CAS; multi-producer mode uses CAS to claim.
  2. Pre-allocated, reused entries: no GC churn on the hot path; events are mutated in place.
  3. Padding: Sequence values are padded so each counter sits on its own cache line (avoids false sharing; see JMM chunk).
  4. Dependency graph: consumers form pipelines (A then B,C in parallel) without extra queues; batching: a consumer processes all available events up to the cursor.
  5. Wait strategies trade CPU for latency (busy spin burns a core).

Compared to ArrayBlockingQueue: one ReentrantLock, head/tail counters sharing cache lines, and park/unpark cost on contention. Reported speedups vary widely by benchmark (several-fold to 10x or more in blog benchmarks); treat any number as workload-specific and benchmark with JMH.

Don't use it when: you need unbounded buffering, dynamic consumers, simple code, or when you can't dedicate cores (busy-spin on a container with a 2-CPU quota hurts everything else).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// LMAX Disruptor 3.x/4.x API (verify version)
Disruptor<LongEvent> d = new Disruptor<>(LongEvent::new, 1024, DaemonThreadFactory.INSTANCE);
d.handleEventsWith((event, seq, endOfBatch) -> process(event.value));
d.start();
d.getRingBuffer().publishEvent((e, s, v) -> e.value = v, 42L);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Holding references in reused events so objects are never freed, or failing to clear them.
  • Busy-spin wait strategy in a CPU-limited container.
  • Adopting it without measuring that the queue is the bottleneck.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is false sharing? → Two threads writing different variables on one cache line cause cache invalidation ping-pong; padding or @Contended separates them.
  2. How does backpressure work? → Producers block/spin when the ring is full relative to the slowest consumer's sequence.
  3. Is it a general replacement for thread pools? → No; it's a pipeline with fixed topology.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "very fast queue". Senior explains the sequence protocol, single writer, preallocation, padding, wait strategies, and when it is overkill.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An order-matching path moved off LinkedBlockingQueue cut p99 handoff latency; an unrelated REST service tried the same and gained nothing since network I/O dominated.

questions.contextHtml: You are designing an ingestion stage: an HTTP endpoint receives ~4,000 events/s (peaks 12,000/s for 30 s), each event needs a 15 ms enrichment (remote call) and then a batched DB insert (500 rows per insert, ~40 ms). The pod has 4 vCPU, 2 GB RAM, -Xmx1200m. The previous version used new Thread(...) per event, then a switch to an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue with 8 consumers; staging OOMed after a peak. Latency target for the HTTP call is p99 < 200 ms; events may be dropped only with an explicit 429. Events cannot be lost once accepted (HTTP 202).
questions.promptHtml: Design the producer-consumer pipeline: queue type and size, consumer count, batching, shutdown, and failure handling.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a BlockingQueue and a thread pool." No capacity math, no backpressure, no shutdown or durability answer.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is "accepted" durable (must survive a pod crash)? Is order per key required? Is the enrichment idempotent? What is max event size? Can the producer retry on 429?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (Not an incident; baseline) cap in-flight data so memory is bounded.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: The constraints decide: durable acceptance means an in-memory queue alone cannot satisfy "never lose after 202". Options: (a) in-memory bounded queue + at-most-once (violates requirement); (b) append to a durable log (Kafka/outbox table) before 202, consumers pull; (c) in-memory with write-ahead file. I'd pick (b) because it also solves backpressure and restart.
  4. How I'd verify each: Capacity math. Consumer service rate: enrichment 15 ms with 16 concurrent calls = ~1,060/s; need 4,000/s sustained so concurrency >= 4,000 x 0.015 = 60 in flight (Little's law). With platform threads that's 60-80 threads (I/O bound) or virtual threads; DB side: 4,000/500 = 8 batches/s x 40 ms = 0.32 busy DB connections, trivial. Peak 12,000/s x 30 s = 360k events surplus ~ (12,000-4,000) x 30 = 240k events; at 1 KB = 240 MB, which fits an in-memory buffer but not safely with 1.2 GB heap alongside everything else; hence bound at e.g. 50k events (~50-100 MB) and spill to the log/429.
  5. Root cause: n/a (design). The failure mode to avoid: arrival > service with an unbounded buffer.
  6. Fix (design):
// bounded handoff, explicit rejection
BlockingQueue<Event> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(50_000);
boolean accepted = q.offer(ev);          // non-blocking on the request thread
if (!accepted) return Response.status(429).header("Retry-After", "1").build();

// consumer: drain up to 500 or 50 ms, then batch insert
List<Event> batch = new ArrayList<>(500);
Event first = q.poll(50, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);
if (first != null) { batch.add(first); q.drainTo(batch, 499); }
if (!batch.isEmpty()) repo.insertBatch(enrich(batch));

Shutdown: stop accepting (readiness down), let consumers drain until queue empty and flush the final batch, then executor.shutdown() + awaitTermination, with a deadline and a fallback persisting leftovers. Poison pill is an alternative signal (B1-Q175). Failure: retry with bounded attempts and exponential backoff, then a dead-letter table; never swallow exceptions in the consumer loop, or the thread dies silently. 7. Prevention: Metrics: queue depth, oldest event age, consumer lag, rejection rate, batch size, insert latency; alert on queue > 70% for 1 min; load test peak 12,000/s for 60 s with a slowed enrichment. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not unbounded queues; not one thread per event; not CallerRunsPolicy here (HTTP threads would do remote calls and break p99). If durability is truly required, an in-memory queue is only a buffer in front of the durable log, not the source of truth.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Per-key ordering? → Shard into N queues by hash(key) % N with one consumer each.
  • Consumer is slow, queue is at 100% for 10 min? → 429s propagate; autoscale on queue depth; check the downstream first.
  • How would virtual threads change the design? → The enrichment fan-out becomes simple blocking code; you'd still bound concurrency with a Semaphore (V1 chunk).

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A team's "durable" queue was an in-memory list; a rolling deploy dropped 90k accepted events. The fix was a 20-line outbox table and the incident review changed what "accepted" meant in the API contract.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: unbounded queue or thread-per-event, no shutdown plan.
  • Hire: bounded queue, 429 backpressure, batching, graceful drain.
  • Strong hire: Little's-law sizing, durability discussion (log/outbox), ordering via sharding, observability, dead-letter handling.

questions.promptHtml: What does Collections.synchronizedList give you, and what does it not? What are the compound-operation and iteration pitfalls?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Quick filter for engineers who believe "synchronized wrapper means thread-safe program".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It wraps each method in synchronized(mutex), so individual operations are atomic and visible. But compound actions (check-then-add, get-then-set, iteration) are not atomic unless I hold the same mutex around the whole sequence. Iterating without synchronized (list) can throw CME or see inconsistent data. For read-mostly use CopyOnWriteArrayList; for maps use ConcurrentHashMap.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Wrapper = decorator with a single mutex (the wrapper itself unless specified). Everything serializes through one lock, so reads block each other too. Streams, forEach on synchronizedList do synchronize forEach but stream() doesn't hold the lock for you.

Documented iteration idiom:

List<String> list = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
synchronized (list) {
    for (String s : list) use(s);
}

Compound action example: if (!list.contains(x)) list.add(x); is a race even though each call is synchronized.

Also: subList, iterator(), listIterator() views aren't synchronized by themselves.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Broken
if (!list.contains(id)) list.add(id);
// Correct
synchronized (list) { if (!list.contains(id)) list.add(id); }
// Or use a set designed for it
Set<String> ids = ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet();
ids.add(id);               // atomic add-if-absent

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Locking on a different object than the wrapper's mutex.
  • Iterating a view (keySet, subList) without the lock.
  • Treating synchronized wrappers as a performance solution.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is Vector similar? → Same per-method locking; legacy.
  2. When is the wrapper fine? → Low contention, short critical sections, small collections, or when you need a consistent size.
  3. Alternatives for queue semantics? → BlockingQueue implementations.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "makes methods synchronized". Senior names compound-action races, iteration locking contract, and the better collection per access pattern.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A synchronizedList of active sessions was iterated by a metrics thread without a lock, producing intermittent CME in logs.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the difference between blocking, obstruction-free, lock-free and wait-free algorithms, and where the JDK's structures fall.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests precise vocabulary and whether you can reason about latency tails versus throughput.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Blocking: a stalled thread holding a lock can stall everyone. Lock-free: some thread always makes progress in a finite number of steps, though a given thread can retry indefinitely. Wait-free: every thread finishes in a bounded number of steps. Obstruction-free: a thread completes if it runs alone. CAS-loop structures like AtomicInteger.updateAndGet, ConcurrentLinkedQueue are lock-free; getAndIncrement on x86 (LOCK XADD) and LongAdder.add in the uncontended path are effectively wait-free per op; ConcurrentHashMap.get is wait-free for readers in practice, but writes use locks.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Blocking       < Obstruction-free < Lock-free < Wait-free     (stronger guarantee ->)

Why it matters:

  • A lock holder pre-empted by the OS or paused at a safepoint or GC blocks all waiters (no lock-free structure suffers priority inversion or a convoy).
  • Lock-free doesn't mean fast: under heavy contention CAS retries waste cycles and cache coherence traffic grows; a lock with parking may give better throughput.
  • Lock-free doesn't guarantee fairness: starvation of one thread is possible.
  • Wait-free algorithms are rare and complex; used where tail latency bounds matter.
  • Lock-free structures complicate memory reclamation in non-GC languages (ABA, hazard pointers); the JVM's GC simplifies this.

JDK examples: ConcurrentLinkedQueue/Deque (lock-free, Michael-Scott variant), ConcurrentSkipListMap (lock-free), AtomicXxx (CAS loop), ConcurrentHashMap (hybrid: CAS for empty bins, locks otherwise), ArrayBlockingQueue (blocking).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Lock-free retry loop (not wait-free): each attempt may fail only if another thread succeeded
int updateMax(AtomicInteger max, int x) {
    int cur;
    do { cur = max.get(); if (x <= cur) return cur; } while (!max.compareAndSet(cur, x));
    return x;
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Equating lock-free with "no waiting" or "always faster".
  • Calling a CAS loop wait-free.
  • Ignoring that lock-free code may still spin and burn CPU.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a lock-free algorithm starve a thread? → Yes, system-wide progress only.
  2. Why prefer lock-free for latency-sensitive paths? → No convoy and no blocking due to a descheduled lock holder.
  3. Does GC pause break lock-freedom? → A stop-the-world pause stops all threads; lock-free helps for per-thread descheduling and safepoint skew, not global pauses.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "lock-free uses CAS". Senior gives the formal hierarchy, classifies JDK structures, and knows lock-free isn't automatically faster.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team replaced a lock around a counter with a CAS loop and saw worse p99 under 64 threads because retries starved some threads.

questions.contextHtml: A gateway (Java 17, 32 vCPU pod, 6,000 RPS per pod, 200 worker threads) records per-request stats in a shared class: AtomicLong totalRequests, AtomicLong totalBytes, AtomicLong errors, all incremented on every request. CPU is 70% with p99 at 45 ms; the SLO is 30 ms and the team wants to avoid adding pods (each costs about 1,400 USD/month; 40 pods). An async-profiler CPU flame graph (-e cpu) shows 11% of samples in AtomicLong.incrementAndGet / Unsafe.getAndAddLong frames, and perf stat shows a high cache-miss rate. A teammate proposes sharding the counters by hand with an array indexed by threadId % 8.
questions.promptHtml: How do you confirm the diagnosis and what would you change? What are the risks?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Atomics are lock-free so they can't be the problem", or hand-rolled striping without considering false sharing and read semantics.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: How often are the counters read (scrape every 15 s)? Does anything depend on the exact value (rate limiting, IDs)? Are the three counters in one object (same cache line)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: None needed for safety; this is optimization. If urgent, reduce per-request counters (aggregate per batch).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) cache-line contention on the three AtomicLongs (likely in one or two lines): 200 threads on 32 cores hammering 18k increments/s... per pod 6,000 RPS x 3 = 18,000/s is low in absolute terms, so contention alone seems modest; (b) the 11% could be misattributed due to safepoint bias or inlined frames; (c) other shared state. Honest check: 18k atomic ops/s is a trivial rate, so I'd be suspicious; real contention shows at millions of ops/s. Unless counters are also touched per-byte or per-event, not per-request.
  4. How I'd verify each: Re-profile with async-profiler (not safepoint-biased), then a JMH micro-benchmark of AtomicLong vs LongAdder with @Threads(32); count increments per request in code (maybe totalBytes.addAndGet per chunk, 40 per request = 720k/s); check object layout with JOL for shared lines.
  5. Root cause: In this scenario the counters were updated per chunk (about 60 times per request), so ~1M ops/s on three adjacent fields: they share a cache line, causing true and false sharing. Each lock xadd pulls the line exclusive between cores.
  6. Fix: Short term: swap to LongAdder and read sum() only in the scrape.
private final LongAdder totalRequests = new LongAdder();
private final LongAdder totalBytes = new LongAdder();
private final LongAdder errors = new LongAdder();
void onChunk(int n) { totalBytes.add(n); }
long bytesSnapshot() { return totalBytes.sum(); }

Long term: aggregate per request locally (one add per request) and use Micrometer, which already uses striped counters internally (verify for the registry in use). 7. Prevention: JMH benchmarks in CI for shared hot paths; code review rule "metrics counters are LongAdder"; periodic continuous profiling (JFR/async-profiler) with a baseline. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not hand-rolled threadId % 8 striping (collisions, false sharing without padding, reinventing Striped64). Don't use LongAdder for anything needing exact check-and-update. Memory cost: up to one cell per core, a few hundred bytes, negligible here. Expected win: remove most of the 11% CPU; at 70% -> ~62% CPU, fewer pods needed at same load; validate with a canary before claiming savings (10% of 40 pods x 1,400 USD = ~5,600 USD/month, if load balancing allows).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if sum() is called per request for a rate limiter? → Then LongAdder is wrong; use a token bucket with CAS or partitioned budgets.
  • Does LongAdder help with 4 threads? → Barely; adds memory and a more complex read path.
  • Why not ThreadLocal<long[]>? → Reading requires registering and iterating all thread locals; leak risk in pools.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: An "optimization" swapped every AtomicLong for LongAdder in a cache; the hit/miss ratio was used to trigger resizing, and sum() calls in the hot path made it slower than before.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: dismisses atomics as never a bottleneck, or proposes hand-sharding.
  • Hire: profiles, benchmarks with JMH, swaps to LongAdder.
  • Strong hire: sanity-checks the rate, notes cache-line placement and non-atomic sum(), quantifies cost and validates with a canary.

questions.contextHtml:
An inventory service (Java 21, 8 vCPU, Tomcat with 200 threads) uses a ConcurrentHashMap<Long, Product> as a read-through cache of 2 million SKUs (table size 4M bins):

Product get(long sku) {
    return cache.computeIfAbsent(sku, id -> catalogClient.fetch(id)); // HTTP, 30 ms typical
}

During a catalog slowdown (fetch 30 ms -> 4 s p99), the service's p99 goes from 60 ms to 25 s, all 200 Tomcat threads are busy, and /health times out so Kubernetes restarts pods. Thread dumps show ~190 threads blocked in ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent, 6 threads in SocketInputStream.read. Hit rate is 97%. Someone says: "97% hit rate, so the lock shouldn't matter".
questions.promptHtml: Why did a 97% hit rate not protect you, and what would you change?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase Tomcat threads or catalog timeout." Misses that the function runs while the bin head is locked and that hits may also queue behind a locked bin.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is fetch timeout-bounded? Are hot SKUs concentrated? Is stale data acceptable during an outage? What is the load per pod?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set a hard 300 ms timeout and fall back to stale/default; shed load via 503 on cache miss; restart is not a fix. Capture jstack first.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) blocking I/O inside computeIfAbsent holds the bin lock; other computeIfAbsent calls for keys in the same bin block, and for a present key computeIfAbsent can also block if the bin is locked in the version in use (Javadoc: other update attempts may be blocked while the computation is in progress; reads via get are not blocked); (b) thread pool starvation from the 4 s fetches (190/200 threads waiting); (c) GC. Dumps match (a)+(b).
  4. How I'd verify each: jcmd Thread.print and group by top frame; count threads per monitor owner (locked <0x...> with the owning thread in SocketInputStream.read); Micrometer for cache misses/s; compare get-path latency.
  5. Root cause: The mapping function executes under the synchronized lock of the bin's first node. Many distinct keys miss concurrently (a catalog refresh made 3% of 6,000 RPS = 180 misses/s x 4 s = ~720 in-flight fetches demand), and any two keys in one bin serialize. Meanwhile computeIfAbsent on an existing key may still take the bin lock in the simple path (implementation-specific: verify in your JDK; since 9 there is a fast path for a first node match without locking), so even hits can stall. Tomcat threads run out, health checks queue, kubelet kills pods, and the restart empties the cache (thundering herd).
  6. Fix:
ConcurrentHashMap<Long, CompletableFuture<Product>> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

CompletableFuture<Product> get(long sku) {
    CompletableFuture<Product> f = cache.get(sku);
    if (f != null) return f;
    CompletableFuture<Product> mine = new CompletableFuture<>();
    CompletableFuture<Product> prev = cache.putIfAbsent(sku, mine);
    if (prev != null) return prev;                  // someone else is loading
    catalogClient.fetchAsync(sku).orTimeout(300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)
        .whenComplete((p, ex) -> {
            if (ex != null) { cache.remove(sku, mine); mine.completeExceptionally(ex); }
            else mine.complete(p);
        });
    return mine;
}

Better: Caffeine AsyncLoadingCache with refreshAfterWrite, expireAfterWrite, and stale-on-error. Bulkhead the catalog call with its own bounded executor/semaphore (e.g. 32 concurrent) and a separate health endpoint thread pool. 7. Prevention: Fault-injection test with a slow dependency; alert on Tomcat busy threads > 80%; lint for I/O in compute lambdas; separate liveness from readiness. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raise Tomcat threads to 800 (more waiting threads, more memory); not remove timeouts. Future-valued maps cache failures if not removed (shown above). On Java 21 virtual threads would make waiting cheaper but not remove the bin lock serialization.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why did restarting make it worse? → Cold cache means 100% misses, a stampede on the catalog.
  • Would get + put have been better? → Yes for locking, but it duplicates loads on a stampede; the future-valued map dedups.
  • Could the hash distribution matter? → Skewed keys or weak hashes concentrate in few bins and amplify blocking.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A cache warm-up at deploy time plus a slow dependency made every pod unhealthy at once; the rolling restart looked like a cascading outage, and the real fix was a 20-line change moving the call out of the map.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: tunes thread counts or timeouts only.
  • Hire: identifies blocking inside compute, uses future-valued cache or Caffeine.
  • Strong hire: explains bin lock mechanics, stampede, bulkhead, timeout, health-check separation, and verification from thread dumps.

questions.contextHtml:
A batch exporter uses one producer thread filling a BlockingQueue<Row> (capacity 1,000) and 4 consumer threads writing to S3. On completion the main thread should flush and exit. In production the job sometimes hangs forever after the producer finishes (about 1 run in 20), and at other times it exits but the last ~800 rows are missing. Code:

volatile boolean done = false;
BlockingQueue<Row> q = new LinkedBlockingQueue<>(1000);

// consumer
while (!done) {
    Row r = q.take();
    write(r);
}
// main
producer.join();
done = true;
pool.shutdownNow();

jstack of the hung run shows consumers in LinkedBlockingQueue.take / AbstractQueuedSynchronizer$ConditionObject.await. An engineer suggests changing take() to poll() in a loop.
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and give a correct shutdown protocol.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Make done volatile" (it already is) or busy-loop with poll(), which burns CPU and still can lose rows.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is the order of shutdown vs. drain important? Can a consumer failure be retried? How many producers?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart the hung job and rerun missing partitions (idempotent writes); take a thread dump first.
  3.
