Hypotheses, ranked: (a) consumers blocked in take() on an empty queue never re-check done, so they hang; (b) shutdownNow() interrupts consumers mid-flight and drops queued rows (the take() throws InterruptedException and the rows in queue aren't written); (c) write swallowing exceptions. Hang 1 in 20 = timing: if the queue happens to be non-empty at the moment, consumers wake and see done.
  4. How I'd verify each: jstack (all consumers parked in take), count rows written vs. produced, log queue size at done = true, add a test with a slow producer.
  5. Root cause: done is only checked between take() calls, while take() blocks indefinitely; and the shutdown interrupts consumers without draining the queue (loss).
  6. Fix: Poison pill, one per consumer, after the producer finishes; consumers exit on seeing it, and the main thread awaits termination (no shutdownNow).
static final Row POISON = new Row(/* sentinel */);

// consumer
try {
    for (Row r; (r = q.take()) != POISON; ) write(r);
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
    Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
}

// main
producer.join();
for (int i = 0; i < CONSUMERS; i++) q.put(POISON);   // FIFO: all real rows precede pills
pool.shutdown();
if (!pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.MINUTES)) { /* log, then pool.shutdownNow() */ }

With multiple producers, send pills only after all producers have finished (CountDownLatch/join all). 7. Prevention: Test with an empty input, with 1 row, and with a slow producer; wrap consumer body in try/catch logging so a thread doesn't die silently; keep sentinel handling in a shared helper. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not poll() busy-wait (CPU) or poll(timeout) + flag unless I also drain properly; poll(timeout) with a done-flag and queue.isEmpty() check is acceptable but racy. Not shutdownNow() as the normal path; it is for timeout/abort.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the queue is full when I try to put the pills? → put blocks until consumers free space; that's fine as consumers are still draining.
  • What if a consumer dies from an exception? → Its pill is unconsumed, so another consumer would receive two; count consumers actually alive, or have a finally that resubmits. Prefer supervising the failure.
  • Alternative to pills? → Close/complete signals: CompletableFuture, or a Phaser/latch with drainTo until empty after producers done.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A nightly exporter "hung" every few weeks; for months the fix was a manual kill. The cause was a done flag checked outside a blocking take(); the fix took 10 minutes once someone read the thread dump.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: busy-wait or more volatile flags.
  • Hire: poison pill per consumer and graceful shutdown/awaitTermination.
  • Strong hire: handles multiple producers, failed consumers, timeouts, data-loss from shutdownNow, and tests edge cases.

questions.promptHtml: What is ConcurrentSkipListMap, how does a skip list give you a concurrent sorted map, and when do you prefer it over ConcurrentHashMap or a synchronized TreeMap?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests knowledge of the only built-in concurrent sorted map and the reasons trees are hard to make concurrent.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: It's a lock-free sorted map (and ConcurrentSkipListSet the set version) built on a skip list: layered linked lists where higher layers skip over many nodes, giving expected O(log n) get/put/remove. Skip lists are easier to make concurrent than balanced trees because inserts and deletes touch only local pointers via CAS and never need global rebalancing. I use it when I need ordered iteration or range queries (headMap, ceilingKey, subMap) under concurrency; otherwise ConcurrentHashMap is faster and lighter.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
L2:  head ----------------> 30 -----------------> null
L1:  head --> 10 ---------> 30 --> 50 -----------> null
L0:  head --> 10 -> 20 ---> 30 -> 40 -> 50 -> 60 -> null

Each node is promoted to higher levels randomly (probability 1/2 per level), so expected height is O(log n). Search starts top-left and drops down. Deletion marks a node's value logically (CAS to null / marker node) then unlinks it physically; other threads help clean up. This is the Harris/Lea-style design; the Javadoc states ops are expected O(log n) and the map is sorted by natural order or a Comparator.

Properties:

  • Weakly consistent iterators in sort order, no CME.
  • size() is O(n) (traverses), not constant.
  • Higher memory per entry than CHM (multiple index nodes) and worse cache locality than arrays/hash tables.
  • Navigation ops (floorEntry, pollFirstEntry) are atomic per call; pollFirstEntry makes a decent concurrent priority/time-ordered structure (e.g. timer wheels, order books).
  • No null keys or values.

vs Collections.synchronizedSortedMap(new TreeMap<>()): one lock, simple, fine at low contention; vs PriorityBlockingQueue: skip list supports removal by key and range scans, queue only head ops.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
ConcurrentSkipListMap<Long, Order> book = new ConcurrentSkipListMap<>();
book.put(price, order);
Map.Entry<Long, Order> best = book.firstEntry();                  // lowest key
NavigableMap<Long, Order> window = book.subMap(lo, true, hi, false);   // live view

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using it where only key lookups are needed (slower than CHM).
  • Calling size() frequently.
  • Relying on a mutable key's comparator ordering changing after insertion.
  • Assuming compound operations on the sub-views are atomic.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why no concurrent red-black tree in the JDK? → Rebalancing rotations touch many nodes, making lock-free or fine-grained designs hard.
  2. Is it O(log n) worst case? → Expected, not worst case (randomized levels).
  3. How would you implement a time-ordered expiry index? → ConcurrentSkipListMap<Long, ...> keyed by (expiry, id) with pollFirstEntry when firstKey() <= now.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3-YOE: "sorted concurrent map". Senior explains skip-list layering, CAS-based marking/unlinking, why trees are hard, memory/locality costs, and O(n) size.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A leaderboard maintained in a synchronized TreeMap serialized 32 threads; moving to ConcurrentSkipListMap helped reads, but writes by hot keys still contended on the same nodes.

questions.contextHtml: A real-time ad service (Java 21, 16 vCPU, 300 worker threads) tracks per-campaign spend in ConcurrentHashMap<String, Long> spend using spend.merge(campaignId, cents, Long::sum). Today: 20k merges/s, p99 4 ms. Marketing plans a launch expected to give 10x traffic with one flagship campaign receiving about 60% of impressions. Load test at 10x (200k merges/s, 120k/s on one key): p99 jumps to 180 ms, CPU in ConcurrentHashMap.merge and monitorenter frames rises, throughput plateaus at 90k/s. Table has 5,000 campaigns. A teammate suggests increasing the CHM initial capacity to 64k "to reduce collisions".
questions.promptHtml: Why does it plateau, will the larger capacity help, and what is your design?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase capacity / use concurrencyLevel / more cores". Doesn't notice that one key means one bin and one lock; sharding the table can't spread a single key.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must spend be exact in real time or can budget checks be approximate? Is the read side per-request (pacing) or periodic? Are updates idempotent/replayable? Is it multi-pod (so the source of truth is elsewhere)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Batch increments per worker (aggregate locally, flush every 50 ms) to cut merge calls on the hot key.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) single hot key means serialized updates under one bin lock (merge does the compute under synchronized); throughput limit = 1 / critical section time, observed ~90k/s ~ 11 µs per op incl. contention handoff; (b) the boxing Long allocation per merge adds GC pressure (200k/s x 16 B = 3.2 MB/s, minor); (c) hash collisions across 5,000 keys (minor at 16k+ bins).
  4. How I'd verify each: async-profiler lock mode (-e lock) showing contention on the bin head node; per-key operation histogram; JMH with a zipf distribution vs uniform; JFR jdk.JavaMonitorEnter events.
  5. Root cause: Capacity helps distribute different keys across bins; it can't split one key. 60% of traffic on one key serializes all those updates on one monitor. Amdahl: 60% serialized => max speedup ~1.67x regardless of threads.
  6. Fix: Keep ConcurrentHashMap for lookup, but make each value a striped counter:
ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> spend = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
void record(String id, long cents) {
    LongAdder a = spend.get(id);
    if (a == null) a = spend.computeIfAbsent(id, k -> new LongAdder());   // rare path
    a.add(cents);                                                         // no bin lock
}

get is lock-free, so the hot path never takes a bin lock; add is striped over cells. For budget enforcement read sum() periodically and use local pacing (each worker gets a budget slice) rather than exact per-request checks. 7. Prevention: Load tests with realistic skew (zipf/hot-key), per-key metric of max updates/s, a code-review rule "no merge/compute on a known-hot key". 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not raising capacity or concurrencyLevel as the fix (does not address the hot key). LongAdder gives approximate reads while writes happen; exact budget cutoffs can overshoot by in-flight amounts; if hard caps are required, use a central atomic reservation with batching (reserve 1,000-cent chunks). Local pre-aggregation adds up to 50 ms of reporting delay and loses data on crash unless replayable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• What if the service has 20 pods? → Then each pod's counter is a local estimate; true spend needs a shared store (Redis/DB) updated in batches.
  • Why not a ThreadLocal counter per worker? → Registration and aggregation complexity; LongAdder already does striping.
  • Will treeification help hot-key collisions? → No; a hot key is a single entry, not a long bin.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A launch-day campaign counter pinned 12 cores on one monitor; the dashboards showed "CPU high, throughput flat". The change from merge to LongAdder values was 6 lines.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: increases capacity or cores.
  • Hire: recognizes single-bin serialization, switches to LongAdder values.
  • Strong hire: applies Amdahl's math, load-tests with skew, discusses approximate reads, budget enforcement and multi-pod truth.

questions.contextHtml: Post-incident review. An event-routing service kept subscriber callbacks in a CopyOnWriteArrayList<Subscriber>. Normally ~200 subscribers with a few changes per hour. A bug in a client library re-registered a new subscriber on every reconnect without unregistering the old one. Timeline: 10:00 a reconnect storm (network flap) starts at 300 reconnects/s across 40 clients; by 10:12 the list holds about 215,000 entries; each add copies the array (215k x 4 bytes compressed refs = ~860 KB). Allocation rate hits 260 MB/s from that alone (300 adds/s x 860 KB), G1 logs Humongous Allocation warnings (region size 2 MB so objects >= 1 MB are humongous; here 860 KB is below, but the list reached 270k entries later, 1.08 MB), young GC pauses rise from 20 ms to 340 ms, event fan-out latency (iterating 215k subscribers per event, many being dead connections) goes from 2 ms to 900 ms, and a "ConcurrentModificationException" alert fired from a different component. Pods OOM at 10:41.
questions.promptHtml: Lead the post-incident review: root causes, contributing factors, why CME appeared elsewhere, and corrective actions.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Bad library, fix the library". Ignores the data-structure choice, the lack of bounds and metrics, and the misleading CME.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Why did the old subscribers stay (strong refs, no heartbeat)? Is a subscriber identity defined (equals)? Do we have list-size metrics? What did the CME come from?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart with a flag to reject duplicate registrations, evict dead connections; disable the faulty client versions; reduce reconnect aggressiveness (server-side backoff).
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) unbounded growth of subscribers (leak) in a structure whose write cost is O(n): CopyOnWriteArrayList.add = O(n) copy + allocation; (b) fan-out cost O(n) per event multiplied by dead subscribers; (c) the CME arises elsewhere: a different class iterated a plain ArrayList copy of the subscriber list being mutated by reconnect handlers, or code used new ArrayList<>(subs) with another structure; (d) G1 humongous allocations (arrays >= half region size) adding fragmentation.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap dump + MAT (retained size of the COW array and the dead Subscriber objects); GC logs -Xlog:gc*,gc+humongous=debug (verify tag); Micrometer gauge subscribers.count; trace the CME stack to its owner; check reconnect logs for duplicate IDs.
  5. Root cause: Registration leak (no dedup, no unregister on disconnect) in a copy-on-write list, whose cost model assumes rare writes and small size. Contributing: no cap, no metrics or alert on size, no reconnect backoff, no TTL/heartbeat eviction. The CME was a separate unsynchronized collection in the audit component; the storm merely exposed the race by making mutation frequent (a data race, not a CME-causing COW list).
  6. Fix: Short term: dedupe on register and remove on disconnect.
private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, Subscriber> subs = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
void register(String id, Subscriber s) {
    Subscriber old = subs.put(id, s);
    if (old != null) old.close();
}
void unregister(String id, Subscriber s) { subs.remove(id, s); }   // remove only if same instance
void fire(Event e) { subs.values().forEach(s -> s.on(e)); }        // weakly consistent, no CME

Long term: weak references or lease/heartbeat expiry, caps per client (e.g. 10), bounded fan-out via per-subscriber queues, server-side reconnect backoff with jitter. 7. Prevention: Alerts on subscriber count and registration rate; contract test that reconnect does not increase count; load test with reconnect storms; review checklist "what is the max size and who removes?" for every long-lived collection. 8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not keep COW and just raise heap (cost model is wrong). A CHM keyed by subscriber id loses insertion order (use if order doesn't matter). Dropping old subscribers on duplicate id could disconnect a legit second session; key by (client, session).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would Collections.synchronizedList have been better? → Write cost O(1), but fan-out requires locking during iteration (blocking writers); fine for small lists, but the leak remains.
  • Why do humongous objects matter here? → In G1 an allocation of at least half a region is humongous, allocated directly in old regions and only reclaimed at cleanup/mixed cycles; the region size depends on heap (1-32 MB, verify), so repeated big arrays cause fragmentation and pressure.
  • How do you prevent noisy-client storms? → Rate-limit registrations per client and apply exponential backoff.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "config listeners" list leaked one lambda per request after a refactor; nobody noticed for weeks because list size wasn't a metric, only GC time looked slightly high until a traffic spike.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the client library only.
  • Hire: identifies leak plus COW write cost, fixes with dedup/unregister and a better structure.
  • Strong hire: separates the CME as a different bug, quantifies copy cost and allocation rate, lists detection/prevention (size metrics, caps, backoff) and a blameless action list.
